nameStory: Round-headed bush clover gets its name from its distinctive flower clusters that form tight, rounded heads at the top of the plant. Unlike many of its sprawling relatives, this species grows as an upright bush, earning it the 'bush clover' part of its name. The scientific name 'capitata' comes from the Latin word for 'head,' referring to those characteristic ball-like flower clusters.
description: Round-headed bush clover is a sturdy, upright wildflower that belongs to the legume family, making it a cousin to beans and peas. This native New England plant typically grows 2-4 feet tall with a bushy, branching habit. Its most striking feature is the dense, creamy-white to pale yellow flower clusters that sit like fluffy pompoms at the tips of its branches. The plant has the typical three-leaflet leaves of many legumes and produces small seed pods later in the season.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, rounded clusters of tiny creamy-white to pale yellow flowers perched at branch tips like fuzzy golf balls. Each cluster feels firm and compact when gently touched, and the individual flowers are so tightly packed you can barely see them separately.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-leaflet compound leaves arranged alternately along stems. Each leaflet is narrow and oval-shaped with a smooth, slightly fuzzy texture that feels soft between your fingers, and they often have a grayish-green color.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, bushy plant that grows 2-4 feet tall with multiple branching stems arising from the base. The plant maintains a neat, rounded shape and doesn't sprawl or vine like some of its relatives.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, flattened seed pods develop after flowering, each containing one or two seeds. The pods are typical of legumes but much smaller than garden peas, and they turn brown and papery when mature.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Sturdy, somewhat woody stems that feel firm to the touch and are often covered with fine, soft hairs. The stems branch frequently in the upper portions where the flower heads form.

habitat: Round-headed bush clover thrives in sunny, open areas with well-drained soils throughout New England. Look for it in old fields, prairie remnants, roadside edges, and disturbed areas where it can get full sun. It's particularly common in sandy or gravelly soils and often grows alongside goldenrods, asters, and native grasses in late-summer wildflower communities.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small, three-leaflet leaves on multiple stems from the base. Young plants are low and bushy with fresh green foliage.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from July through September when the distinctive round, creamy-white flower heads appear at branch tips. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and develop into small brown seed pods. Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping, and the dried flower heads often persist.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems remain standing with dried seed pods and old flower heads, creating winter interest and providing food for birds.

funFact: Like all legumes, round-headed bush clover has a secret superpower: it can actually make its own fertilizer! Special bacteria living in tiny nodules on its roots capture nitrogen from the air and convert it into plant food, which is why legumes can thrive in poor soils where other plants struggle.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other bush clovers, especially hairy lespedeza, but round-headed bush clover's flower heads are distinctly round and compact rather than loose or elongated. Remember: 'round-headed' means round flower heads - if the flowers are in loose clusters or spikes, it's probably a different species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'clover,' bush clovers are not closely related to the familiar white and red clovers of lawns and fields. True clovers belong to the genus Trifolium, while bush clovers are in the genus Lespedeza, though both are members of the large legume family.
compareHints: Round-headed bush clover stands out from its Lespedeza relatives by its distinctly round, compact flower heads - most other bush clovers have loose, elongated flower clusters or flowers scattered along the stems. It's also more upright and bushy than trailing species like creeping lespedeza, and its flower heads are much more densely packed than the loose spikes of hairy lespedeza. The key is in the name: truly round flower heads are this species' signature feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's bush clovers, hairy lespedeza stands out for its distinctly fuzzy, velvety texture covering the entire plant.
Among its bush clover relatives, violet bush clover stands out with its smooth (not hairy) stems and leaves, and its loose flower arrangement rather than dense round clusters.
Among New England's bush clovers, Chinese bushclover stands out for its silvery, densely hairy appearance and aggressive colonial growth habit.
Among New England's bush clovers, slender bush clover stands out for its delicate, wispy appearance with thin stems and small flower clusters.

Among its bush-clover relatives, tall bush-clover stands out with its reliably erect stems - round-headed bush clover has similar upright growth but denser, more rounded flower clusters, while violet bush clover and trailing lespedeza have more sprawling or leaning growth habits.
Among the many Lespedeza species, shrub lespedeza is unique in New England for its tall, shrubby growth habit - most other bush clovers in our region are low-growing or trailing plants.
Unlike its upright relatives like round-headed bush clover or hairy lespedeza that can reach several feet tall, trailing lespedeza never gets off the ground.
Among its bush clover relatives, narrow-leaved bush clover stands out for its distinctly slender leaflets and preference for wet soils.
Among the bush clovers in New England, violet bush clover stands out for its distinctly purple-violet flowers - most of its relatives have white, cream, or very pale pink blooms.
Among the lespedezas, Thunberg's is unique for its dramatic weeping form - most other bush clovers in New England grow upright or spreading but not with these long, graceful drooping branches.
While most of its lespedeza relatives like round-headed bush clover and violet bush clover grow upright in bushy clumps, creeping lespedeza is the ground-hugger of the family.
Downy lespedeza stands out from other bush clovers in New England primarily by its extremely fuzzy, silvery appearance.
